A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Evolutionary Prediction Games by the same authors. Their complete main texts, figures, equations, references, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic simulations and neural-network experiments on CIFAR-10 and MNIST, including results in the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds three-group evolutionary-dynamics simulations in Figures 6 and 8.

M1.justification: Section 3 adds optional group-specific retention functions, transforming expected accuracy into fitness and extending the population-response model. The learning algorithms and reflected-state stabilization procedure A'(p) = A(2p* - p) already appear in v1 and remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds synthetic three-group populations with distinct distributions and with two identical distributions (Figures 6 and 8). The existing two-group constructions, noisy-label MNIST task, and original-versus-flipped CIFAR-10 task remain.

E2.justification: The CIFAR-10 comparison between ordinary and stabilized retraining is retained. The SVM variants and k-NN choices are also unchanged. The new three-group simulations introduce no additional comparison method; 'oracle' replaces 'optimal' terminology.

E3.justification: The added three-group analyses evaluate replicator flows over a two-dimensional simplex and include identical distributions as an explicit equivalence control. The retained neural-network experiments report the same training and testing settings. The newly specified CIFAR-10 interpolation grid is additional documentation, not evidence of a revised existing protocol.

E4.justification: Figures 6 and 8 add analyses of restricted equilibria and the consequences of oracle-equivalent groups. The earlier Soft-SVM regularization bifurcations and k-NN neighbor-number analyses are retained as v2 Figures 9 and 10.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without repetition counts or confidence intervals. v2 Section 6 reports 50 MNIST repetitions and 20 CIFAR-10 repetitions, with uncertainty bounds; Appendix E specifies normal mean confidence intervals at 99% confidence. This establishes new reporting, not an increase in runs.

E6.justification: New results include seven fixed points in the distinct three-group simulation and stable mixtures of equivalent groups in Figure 8. The main reported accuracy estimates remain unchanged: CIFAR-10 92.6% versus 93.5%, and MNIST 80.4% test accuracy and 98.7% training accuracy.

T1.justification: v2 adds behavioral microfoundation derivations, revises the dynamics assumptions, and introduces oracle-equivalence definitions and guarantees (Appendix D.5.1) plus heterogeneous-retention results (D.5.2). The principal theorem explicitly states monotonic accuracy along trajectories and qualifies single-group exclusion. The existing SVM, k-NN, and stabilization proofs are largely retained or relocated.

C1.justification: The central idealized-exclusion versus practical-coexistence message remains. However, Section 4 qualifies the exclusion guarantee by allowing groups sharing an oracle classifier and optimal accuracy to coexist, and extends the claimed guarantees to heterogeneous retention. These refine the scope of the main theoretical contribution.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly makes coexistence's desirability context-dependent, interprets other groups as a source of regularization, and cautions against treating proxy losses as a prescription for coexistence. It also develops behavioral interpretations through microfoundations. The original impact and limitations discussion is retained in Appendix A.

D1.justification: Appendix E newly documents the explicit discrete replicator update, the CIFAR-10 population grid in 0.1 increments, and matplotlib/mpltern usage. Architecture specifications, hardware, runtimes, and the code-access link are largely retained. These disclosures do not establish changes to the underlying retained experiments.

R1.justification: Related-work coverage substantially expands beyond v1's brief discussion. v2 develops connections to forecasting and proper scoring rules, long-term fairness, and dynamics-aware learners. Appendix B directly distinguishes its guarantees from Hashimoto et al.'s assumptions about incoming users and local stability, providing substantially sharper research positioning.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, the setting and dynamics discussion are reorganized, and the empirical subsections are reversed. Training-once, interpolation, and finite-data discussions move into the appendices. Terminology changes include 'optimal' to 'oracle' and 'beneficial coexistence' to 'mutualism.'

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, with extensive resizing and redistribution of figures and equations. The four-scenario schematic moves from v1 Figure 2 to appendix Figure 5. Two new ternary phase diagrams add flow arrows, accuracy color scales, and equilibrium markers; existing figures receive revised captions and labels.

improvement.justification: v2 improves scope qualification, behavioral motivation, uncertainty reporting, and reproducibility documentation. However, the new heterogeneous-retention welfare guarantee has a proof defect: on PDF page 27, the B-group term differentiates with respect to p_A but multiplies by -dot(p_A), giving an incorrect chain-rule sign. This leaves an important added guarantee unsupported. The explanatory and empirical gains coexist with this theoretical regression, preventing a reliable net-quality judgment.
